summary: Registers two media feature tags, charset and language.

plainLanguage.summary: This adds two labels to the list of device abilities: which letters it can show and which language it uses.

questions: charset and language media feature tags
what is the charset media feature tag
what is the language media feature tag
subtitle: Registers two media feature tags so devices can say which character sets and human languages they handle.

tldr.problem: Devices and protocols that describe their abilities needed standard tags for the character sets a device can display and the human languages it or its user understands.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fills in registration templates for two media feature tags, charset and language, each with an ASN.1 identifier, value rules and examples.
tldr.outcome: Any protocol that uses media feature tags can now express charset and language abilities with these two registered names.

today: RFC 2987 is a Proposed Standard from November 2000. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What Is Being Registered
sections.content:
This document is almost entirely a pair of registrations. It registers two media feature tags, charset and language, which let a device describe the character sets and human languages that it and its user can understand. The templates are derived from RFC 2506, the media feature tag registration procedure.

Both registrations say they are intended for any protocol that uses media tags, both have intended usage COMMON, and both name the IETF as author and change controller. The contact for both is Paul Hoffman.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a form for new labels. This memo fills the form out twice, once for the letters a device can show and once for its language.

sections.title: The charset Tag
sections.content:
The charset tag has ASN.1 identifier 1.3.6.1.8.1.31. It indicates the ability to display particular charsets as defined in RFC 2978. For most devices it is usually a capability, because most devices cannot intelligently process text in a charset they do not know.

Values are tokens defined in that RFC. They can only be compared for equality, and the comparison is not case sensitive. The RFC's example is a weighted list: (| (charset=utf-8);q=1.0 (charset=iso-8859-1);q=0.9 (charset=utf-16);q=0.5 ).
sections.plainLanguage: The charset label tells others which alphabets and symbol sets the device can draw on its screen. Unknown ones turn into gibberish, so it matters.

sections.title: The language Tag
sections.content:
The language tag has ASN.1 identifier 1.3.6.1.8.1.32. It indicates the ability to display particular human languages as defined in RFC 1766. Here "display" will most often mean speech by a computer, and for most devices the feature is a preference, not a requirement.

Values are tokens whose allowed values come from language tag registration. Language tags are handled as a single token and subtags are not used for comparison. Comparison is for equality only and is not case sensitive. The example is (| (language=no-nynorsk);q=1.0 (language=no-bokmaal);q=0.9 (language=i-sami-no);q=0.5 ).
sections.plainLanguage: The language label says which spoken or written languages a person likes, in order of favorite, such as Norwegian first.

sections.title: Interoperability Advice
sections.content:
For both tags, the RFC advises writing values in all lowercase letters, even though names are not case sensitive, to make interoperability more likely.

For charset, aliases should not be used in media feature expressions, because tools that manipulate expressions may convert aliases to the principal charset name. The charset capability should always be indicated together with any capability to handle textual data.
sections.plainLanguage: Write the labels in small letters and use the main name, not a nickname, so everyone reads them the same way.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Each registration carries the same kind of note. If a security bug is known in how a particular charset or language is displayed in a particular environment, knowing that a device accepts it may slightly help an attacker. The document's own Security Considerations section just points back to the two registrations.

The IANA Considerations section is one line: the bulk of the document is IANA registrations. Both registrations request no IANA publication delay.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone knows your device shows a certain alphabet and that alphabet has a bug, they might use that. The risk is small.
